findings.attack: Cross-cutting: is the claim right that A1, A3 and A5 succeeded before hardening, and only those? Did the interface block them?
findings.problem: The task's pointer is wrong: HEAD~1 (0dd2652) is the hardening commit, so 'git show HEAD~1:services/access_service.py' returns the hardened file. The real pre-hardening file is HEAD~2 (b1468b7). I loaded the HEAD~2 service into memory and ran all 13 tests against it. Exactly A1, A3 and A5 fail, which matches evidence/adversarial_2026-10-01/before_hardening.txt. Pre-hardening, A1 and A3 return a full ALLOW=True on all five predicates, and A5's check_scope returns True. app.py and every other service are byte-identical between HEAD~2 and HEAD, so the interface guards did exist before the fix. A1: the guardian picker at app.py:304 only offers consent.guardian_dids. A3: app.py:307-309 refuses a second signature from the same DID. A5: app.py:460-462 stops on an empty request scope. That guard was a commented-out block until commit 4627a1d (24 Sep 08:23); evidence/poc_2026-09-24/README.md row 09 says the empty request 'used to be granted'. A4 was also blocked by the interface (app.py:441-445, choices limited to consent.scope) and by the service both before and after the fix. Caveats: (a) The interface block for A1 is only nominal. There is no authentication of any role (sidebar selectbox, app.py:141-144). Anyone can pick a guardian in G and click Sign, and the server signs for them with a key derived from the DID (app.py:310; identity_service.py:13,21-22). (b) The hardening is in evaluate_allow only. state_service.py:19 and the mint trigger at app.py:281/343 still count raw len(consent.signatures). A duplicate or outside-G consent would therefore still show as ACTIVE and get an SBT minted, though ALLOW would be false. (c) full_suite.txt '36 passed' matches the 13+6+5+4+5+3 test functions in tests/.
findings.wording_constraint: Say 'A1, A3 and A5 succeeded against the service-layer functions (evaluate_allow, check_scope) when called directly in unit tests. They were not reachable through the Streamlit interface as shipped on 24 Sep (app.py:304, 307-309, 460-462).' Do not say the attacks succeeded end to end. For A5, add that the interface guard dates from 4627a1d; before it, the empty request was granted through the UI. Also note that an empty grant discloses no records, because query_patient with [] returns nothing. Note that A4 was also blocked by the interface and was never a service-layer weakness. Cite HEAD~2, not HEAD~1, as the pre-hardening baseline. Do not claim the interface 'enforced' guardian membership: it only restricts the label, and guardians are not authenticated. State that the state machine and the anchoring trigger were not hardened.

findings.attack: A1: a signer outside the guardian set G submits a valid signature to reach the threshold N
findings.problem: The test does exercise the counting rule in evaluate_allow. Z's EIP-712 signature is valid, so VI stays True and the test isolates VA. The assertion (VA False and ALLOW False) is not vacuous, because test_baseline_allows shows that the same fixture with A and B gives ALLOW True, and the pre-hardening code returned ALLOW True. What it proves: after hardening, only distinct DIDs listed in consent.guardian_dids count towards N. What it does NOT prove: that an outsider cannot obtain valid approvals. Guardian keys are keccak('HALAH-DEMO-GUARDIAN-KEY-v1|'+DID) (identity_service.py:13,21-22). I computed B's key from that public derivation, forged B's approval, and the hardened evaluate_allow returned ALLOW=True. It also does not test G itself being set by an attacker: the patient types G freely at app.py:163 and threshold = len(G) (consent_service.py:55).
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'A1 shows that approvals from DIDs outside G are not counted.' Do not write 'an outsider cannot forge approval.' Under the prototype's demo key model, any party that knows a guardian DID can derive that guardian's signing key. The adversary model for A1 must therefore exclude key derivation: it holds only its own key. The fix is a counting fix, not an authentication fix.

findings.attack: A2: replay of a guardian's signature produced for a different consent
findings.problem: The test is genuine. The EIP-712 message binds consentId and the guardian DID, and VI is only computed because the test passes verify_sig. Both the direct verify_signature call and VI=False/ALLOW=False are asserted, with a baseline positive control. It passed before and after hardening. What it does NOT prove: (a) The approval binds only (consentId, guardian, 'APPROVE') (identity_service.py:16,30-32), not scope, purpose, requester, expiry or jurisdiction. I widened scope to all four modules, extended expiry by 10 years and changed requester_did after signing, and ALLOW stayed True. (b) There is no nonce and no verifyingContract in the domain. (c) evaluate_allow checks signatures only when verify_sig is supplied. Called without it (the default, also used by tools/collect_metrics.py:83), a consent with an empty signature_data gives ALLOW=True. app.py:414 does supply it.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'replay across consent identifiers is rejected.' Do not write 'signatures cannot be replayed' or 'approvals are bound to the consent terms'. State explicitly that changing the consent terms after approval is not detected, because the signed message covers the consent ID only. Signature checking applies only on the code path that passes verify_sig (the interface does).

findings.attack: A3: the same guardian approves twice to reach the threshold
findings.problem: This is the right component and the right attack. signature_data holds one valid signature from A, so VI is True and VA is isolated. The assertion is non-vacuous: pre-hardening gave ALLOW True. It proves that evaluate_allow now counts distinct guardian DIDs. It does not show the attack was reachable through the UI: app.py:307-309 rejects a duplicate DID, and that guard existed since ce8d853 (22 Sep). evaluate_state (state_service.py:19) and the SBT mint trigger (app.py:343, len(signatures)==threshold) still count raw list length. A duplicated list injected into storage would therefore still be labelled ACTIVE and anchored, but denied by the matrix.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'A3 succeeded against evaluate_allow at unit level and was already blocked by the guardian interface (app.py:307-309).' Say the fix makes the decision function independent of that UI guard. Do not claim the consent lifecycle, the state labels or on-chain anchoring were hardened.

findings.attack: A4: requested scope S_R is not a subset of the authorised scope S_C
findings.problem: Only check_scope is called. Scope is not part of evaluate_allow's VI..VL matrix; it enters only through authorize() at app.py:488-502. The request partly overlaps S_C (Observation in, Procedure out), which is a good choice. Weakness: the test has no positive control for check_scope. A check_scope that always returned False would pass it, and test_baseline_allows exercises only evaluate_allow. I confirmed separately that check_scope returns True for ['Observation']. Before and after hardening the result is identical, and the UI offers only consent.scope as choices (app.py:441-445). AccessRequest.doctor_did is filled from consent.requester_did (app.py:480-486), not from an authenticated caller.
findings.wording_constraint: Report A4 as 'rejected by check_scope (and also unreachable through the interface, which only offers authorised modules)'. Do not present scope as part of the C=(I,A,P,T,L,E) decision matrix. Note that the requester's identity is not authenticated, so A4 does not show that an unauthorised requester is refused. Ideally add a positive-control assertion before reporting.

findings.problem: This is a real logic flaw at function level: the empty set is a subset of every set, so check_scope returned True at HEAD~2. The fix adds len>0, and the test calls check_scope directly. As with A4, there is no positive control, so an always-False check_scope would pass. Impact before the fix was a vacuous grant with no disclosure: query_patient(did, []) iterates over nothing (database/repository.py:68). The interface has refused an empty request since 4627a1d (app.py:460-462), as screenshot 09 in evidence/poc_2026-09-24 shows.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'A5 was also blocked by the interface before the fix (app.py:460-462, since 24 Sep, commit 4627a1d). The service-layer fix is defence in depth.' Describe the pre-fix outcome as a GRANTED decision with no records released, not as a data leak. Do not claim it was exploitable through the UI on the 24 Sep prototype.

findings.attack: A6: request before notBefore or after expiry
findings.problem: This exercises VT in evaluate_allow for both sides of the interval, with a baseline positive control. It is non-vacuous and passed both before and after the fix. Time comes from datetime.now() on the server, which is trusted, using naive local timestamps. The exact boundary is not tested. evaluate_state and the on-chain checkValid VT are not exercised here: A12 only checks checkValid True and False after revoke.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'the off-chain VT predicate denies requests outside [start, expiry] as measured by the server clock'. The adversary model must exclude control of the server clock. Do not cite A6 as evidence of on-chain temporal enforcement.

findings.attack: A7: the requester declares a jurisdiction different from the consent's
findings.problem: VL is tested with a positive control (AU allows, US denies). But the requester jurisdiction is a self-declared selectbox (app.py:413) passed straight to evaluate_allow (app.py:414). A requester in the US who selects 'AU' passes; I confirmed ALLOW=True. A consent with jurisdiction '' allows any jurisdiction (access_service.py:53-54). The test header says A7 is 'additionally evidenced on-chain by tools/verify_poc'. The only raw checkValidAt(AU)=True / (US)=False output in the repo comes from a local Hardhat chain, chainId 31337 (evidence/poc_2026-09-24/chain.txt:2,31). The Sepolia evidence for VL (sepolia_deploy_v3_2026-09-24.txt) is the app's off-chain decision (SA vs AU), not an on-chain read. The on-chain checkValidAt is never consulted on the access path.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'A7 shows the VL predicate is applied consistently to the declared jurisdiction'. Do not write 'a requester from another jurisdiction is blocked': jurisdiction is self-asserted and unauthenticated, so a dishonest requester defeats VL. Any 'on-chain' VL claim must say local Hardhat EVM (chainId 31337, 24 Sep), not Sepolia. Say that on-chain checkValidAt is not part of the access decision.

findings.problem: Only the local boolean consent.revoked is tested, with a baseline positive control. evaluate_allow does not read chain state. Setting revoked back to False restores ALLOW=True, so whoever can write the SQLite consent row can undo a revocation without anyone noticing. The test does not exercise the revoke flow (app.py:241-249) or the contract. On-chain revocation is evidenced separately on Sepolia (24 Sep, tx 0x017efb9d..., summarised in sepolia_deploy_v3_2026-09-24.txt) and on local Hardhat (chain.txt), produced by other tools on an earlier date.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'a consent marked revoked in the local store is denied by VA'. Keep the on-chain revocation evidence (24 Sep, separate run) apart from the A8 test result. State that the access decision relies on the local flag, not on the chain, so the adversary model excludes write access to the consent store.

findings.attack: A9: tampered Groth16 proof or public signal
findings.problem: This is a real snarkjs Groth16 verification against zk/build/verification_key.json. Flipping publicSignals[1] (the commitment; signals are [ok, commitment, now]) or pi_a[0] is rejected, and the untampered proof is accepted first, so the test is non-vacuous. It skips silently if the zk build is missing; the evidence shows PASSED. What it does NOT prove: verify_proof(proof) takes no consent (zk_service.py:42-49). It never checks the commitment against a registered value or that the public 'now' is current. In the app the server generates and immediately verifies its own proof (app.py:477, 494), so the proof is not an adversary-facing boundary. The trusted setup is a single-party dev setup with time-based entropy (zk/build_zk.sh:9-13). In placeholder mode any non-empty digest verifies.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'the Groth16 verifier rejects bit-level tampering with a proof or its public signals (dev trusted setup)'. Do not write that the proof binds access to a specific consent, to the current time, or to the requester. Do not describe the ZK step as protecting the access decision against an external adversary: in the prototype the prover and verifier are the same server process.

findings.attack: A10: proof for an expired consent
findings.problem: The test asserts only pytest.raises(RuntimeError). Any node or snarkjs failure would also satisfy it. I checked the actual error: 'Assert Failed ... ConsentValidity line 20' (le.out === 1), so in this run it fails for the right reason, but the test does not pin that. More important, the prover chooses both 'now' and 'expiry'. generate_proof(expired_consent, now_ts=3 days ago) produced a proof that verify_proof accepted. Inflating consent.expiry_date before proving also verifies, because the commitment is recomputed and overwritten on every call (zk_service.py:35-36; prove.js:4).
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'the honest prover, using the server clock and the stored expiry, cannot generate a proof for an expired consent'. Do not write 'an expired consent cannot be proven'. An adversarial prover that backdates 'now' or substitutes 'expiry' produces a valid proof, because the verifier checks neither freshness nor a pre-registered commitment.

findings.attack: A11: an attacker modifies a recorded audit event
findings.problem: The test is tautological. It builds a dict, hashes it, changes 'result', and observes a different SHA-256. It never calls audit_db.log, reads the SQLite audit table, or runs any verifier; nothing in the app recomputes digests (event_digest appears only in audit_db.py and a format check in test_halah.py). The digest is unkeyed and unchained, stored in the same row, and covers only actor_did, action, patient_did, consent_id, result and timestamp (audit_db.py:11-13). Changing scope, metadata (decision_matrix, zk_proof_verified), actor_role, purpose or tx_hash leaves it unchanged; I confirmed each. An attacker who rewrites DENIED to GRANTED can recompute event_digest, and deleting or reordering events is undetectable. DATA_ACCESS events are never anchored on chain.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'a change to one of the six digested fields changes that event's digest, so it can be detected only by comparing against a copy of the digest held separately'. The per-event digest is not chained or keyed and does not cover scope or metadata. The ledger is therefore not tamper-evident against anyone with write access to the store, and deletions are not detected. Do not say 'ledger tampering is detected'.

findings.attack: A12: mint, revoke or transfer from an account that is not the owner
findings.problem: This is strong evidence for the contract's access control. I recompiled contracts/ConsentSBTv3.sol in memory (solc 0.8.24, optimizer 200, OZ 4.9.6) and it is byte-identical to blockchain/abi/ConsentSBTv3.json. The test runs on eth-tester's in-memory EVM. It has positive controls (owner mint, checkValidAt AU True / US False, owner revoke then checkValid False). It uses a broad pytest.raises(Exception), but I confirmed the reverts are the intended ones: 'Ownable: caller is not the owner' and 'Soulbound Token'. Not tested: burn by a non-authorised account (I checked it reverts with 'burn not authorised'), safeTransferFrom, transferOwnership and renounceOwnership. The Sepolia v3 contract was compiled separately in Remix (solc 0.8.34) per evidence/sepolia_deploy_v3_2026-09-24.txt, so A12 did not test the deployed bytecode. Security rests on one owner EOA (PRIVATE_KEY on the app server). On-chain checkValid/checkValidAt is never used by the access decision.
findings.wording_constraint: Write 'simulated on an in-memory EVM (eth-tester) with the repository's compiled artifact, not on Sepolia; no Sepolia transaction was sent'. Say the deployed Sepolia bytecode came from a separate Remix build. The result holds only while the single owner key is uncompromised. Do not imply that on-chain state gates data access in the prototype.

findings.attack: Cross-cutting: test header and evidence provenance
findings.problem: The test header says 'A7/A8 are additionally evidenced on-chain by tools/verify_poc'. That evidence is from 24 Sep, a week before the suite, and comes from separate tools. The raw verify_poc output in the repo is from local Hardhat (31337), and the Sepolia result is a prose summary. The 13 tests are unit tests on hand-built Consent objects. None drives app.py, the SQLite store, or the Streamlit session. I re-ran the suite as allowed: 13 passed in 5.03 s. data/halah.db was unchanged (sha256 256b30fa...), because tests/conftest.py redirects HALAH_DB_PATH to a temp file.
findings.wording_constraint: Call these 'unit-level adversarial tests of the decision functions and the contract', not penetration tests of the deployed system. Date the on-chain A7/A8 corroboration (24 Sep) and name the network for each item: local Hardhat 31337 or Sepolia 11155111. Report pass counts as observed in a single environment.

threat_model_scope:
The evidence supports a narrow model: unit-level tests that assume honest infrastructure. In scope is an adversary who can supply crafted inputs to the Python decision functions. That covers a consent record whose signature list includes a non-guardian DID or a duplicate, a signature produced for another consent ID, a request scope that is empty or too wide, a declared jurisdiction that does not match, and a consent outside its validity window or flagged revoked. The same adversary can flip bits in a Groth16 proof or its public signals, and can send transactions to ConsentSBTv3 from a non-owner account on an in-memory EVM (eth-tester, repository artifact byte-identical to the source; not Sepolia). The following are outside what the evidence supports, so the report must state them as exclusions:
(1) Interface-level impersonation. The Streamlit app authenticates no role (app.py:141-144). It signs as any guardian selected in the picker (app.py:304-318), and it takes the requester's identity and jurisdiction from the consent or a self-declared selectbox (app.py:413, 480-486).
(2) Knowledge of the demo key derivation. Guardian keys are keccak of a public tag plus the DID, so anyone can forge approvals.
(3) Write access to the SQLite consent or audit store. The revocation flag is local and can be reset. The audit digest is unkeyed and unchained, covers only six fields, and no component verifies it.
(4) A malicious ZK prover. The verifier binds neither the consent commitment nor the time, and in the app the server proves and verifies for itself.
(5) Manipulation of the server clock.
(6) Changes to consent terms after approval. Signatures bind only the consent ID.
(7) Compromise of the contract owner key, and any network or chain-level behaviour on Sepolia. The deployed Sepolia bytecode came from a separate Remix build, and on-chain state is not consulted in the access decision.
Within this scope, the before/after evidence shows three function-level flaws (A1 and A3 in evaluate_allow, A5 in check_scope) that the interface already blocked as shipped on 24 Sep. The fixes make the decision functions safe without relying on those UI guards; the state machine and the anchoring trigger were not hardened.
